Exactly 100 years after Moore herself visited Cambridge, the purpose of the conference is to bring together an international and various group of readers with a strong predilection for thinking and writing about poetry, and put them to work newly and again on this singular, difficult, and discriminating poet. The schedule will take shape around readings between Marianne Moore and other writers.

items.excerpt: The idea of home is curious concept for African Americans. Though integral to the development and sustainability of the United States, the social death and cultural trauma of slavery render this country inhospitable to Black bodies and the psyches that inhabit them. items.fullDescription: The idea of home is curious concept for African Americans. Though integral to the development and sustainability of the United States, the social death and cultural trauma of slavery render this country inhospitable to Black bodies and the psyches that inhabit them. African Americans are both at home and homeless. This tenuousness places them in a liminal space in which identity is simultaneously self-asserted and assigned, multifaceted, while limited, a fount of agency and a tool for impotence. The intersectional nature of Black femininity further complicates notions of identity and American hospitality. Black men have unsuccessfully employed patriarchy as an intraracial tool to combat the aforementioned social death.

items.fullDescription: Rome and Capri, 21–28 June, 2027 F. Scott Fitzgerald visited Italy on two distinct occasions: first in the spring of 1921 during his and Zelda’s long-deferred honeymoon trip, and again from late 1924 to early 1925 during his unsuccessful attempt to economize. While the Fitzgeralds made brief stops in Venice, San Remo, Portofino, Savona, Pisa, Fiesole, Florence, and Naples, it was in the two host sites of this conference—Rome and Capri—that he spent the most time. It was here that he found inspiration for some of his most celebrated works, as well as several others that remain underexplored.

items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.fullDescription: We invite you to submit an abstract and bio for the panel “ Yesteryear: Cultural and Literary Possibilities”. We are seeking papers that address Caro Claire Burke’s breakout debut novel Yesteryear and its implications on literature and current American culture. How does Burke address established literary conventions? How might one conceive of the evocative narrative style of this novel? How does Burke conceptualize the conscription of motherhood, suppressed queerness, and conservative Christianity? How might the work fit into literary genealogies of sanity, purity, racial prejudice, and womanhood? Proposals should include a title, abstract, your name, and affiliation.

items.fullDescription: The Société Rencesvals, Pan-American Branch, invites proposals from scholars whose research examines Romance-language epics as sites of social discourse. Far from being merely “songs of deeds,” these texts were critical commentaries on contemporary ideologies. They thus speak profoundly to processes of self-conceptualization in far-ranging topics including –but not limited to– regional/national identity, faith, gender, and race. We are interested in the examination of how Romance-language epics use discourse to construct value systems that contribute to conceptions of the self, situating this literature in the larger study of the production of ideologies in the Middle Ages.

items.fullDescription: Plastic / Plasticity Literature and Culture and the Material of a (Bygone?) Era Plastic is a defining material of our era. Its properties—plasticity, durability, the ability to imitate any shape, its toxicity, and indecomposability—are also properties of contemporary culture and literature. The proposed thematic issue begins with the premise that plastic can be read simultaneously as a historical substance and as a "theory machine"—a tool for understanding cultural texts and the experience of contemporary times. "My approach, in this paper, is one of thinking with plastic through its metaphoricity and materiality, its relationality and gestationality; in short, a material mediality.” [R. Gosh]

items.fullDescription: The Department of English-Language Literatures and Cultures and the Institute of Literary Studies at UWM are pleased to invite you to an international interdisciplinary conference on H.G. Wells and Modernity: Texts, Contexts, (Re)visions 22nd-24th Oct. 2026 University of Warmia and Mazury in Olsztyn, Poland Celebrating H.G. Wells's 160th/80th anniversaries of birth and death (1866-1946), this conference invites scholars from across literary studies, linguistics, film studies, political theory, sociology, history, philosophy, and other disciplines to examine modernity's (con)texts through Wells, his contemporaries, and his followers. We aim to consider how their visions reshape understandings of the evolution and devolution of the human, humanity, and society. In many of his literary and non-literary texts, Wells diagnosed the shortcomings of class structures and anticipated modernity's ills, imaginatively prefiguring many current ways of conceptualising the human in relation to the nonhuman. He started as one of the most prolific and versatile short story writers of the late nineteenth century, and he ended as one of the most celebrated sociological and political writers of the first half of the twentieth century. His views, shaped by a complex and troubled faith in science and reason, helped crystallize the formulation of pivotal documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. He died disillusioned that the new world which he had envisioned had not arrived, or worse, frustrated to see his darkest predictions materialise. Undermined and still overlooked as a literary figure by the modernists, who could not see eye to eye with him despite initial friendships, who is H.G. Wells for posterity, that is, our times? In asking this question, we recognize that Wells's legacy cannot be confined to Anglophone literary history alone, and it still speaks urgently to contemporary crises of technology, social fragmentation and political imagination. We especially welcome approaches that could help us position Wells and other modernity/modernist writers within transnational literary networks and explore their influence on and dialogue with world literatures. These topics and others are most welcome, among the proposed conference focus points related to H.G. Wells: ? Author's sources: from antiquity to Jonathan Swift, Charles Dickens, Edgar Allan Poe, and others. ? Modernity and the new ways of writing: short story, scientific romance, science fiction. ? Modern aesthetics and the fictional world: literary and linguistic patterns. Representations of the human and humanity: ecocritical, cognitive, postcolonial, and other postmodern and post-postmodern re-readings. ? Wells and international fantastic and science fiction: comparative perspectives across French (Jules Verne), German, and other contexts. ? Wells's legacy in Polish literature: Stanis?aw Lem and others. ? Dialogues and contentions with Joseph Conrad, E.M. Forster, Virginia Woolf, and Henry James. ? Literary and linguistic depictions of science, catastrophe, and war. ? Shifting cultural concepts: evolution and devolution, tensions of power, ambiguities of colonial appropriation. ? Intermedia reinterpretations: film, graphic novels, games, and other media. ? Wells in translation. ? Political thought and the concept of world state. ? Models of femininity and social change. ? Wells and his engagement with history and the future. ? Utopias and dystopias of Wells and other writers. items.fullDescription: Congreso Estética(s) del Horror: Filosofía, Cine y Literatura. Invitación a envío de propuestas. Congreso presencial (English version below) En los últimos años, el terror ha experimentado una renovada visibilidad cultural. El éxito del cine reciente, la consolidación de una auténtica edad de oro de las series televisivas y la aparición de nuevas voces literarias, impulsadas también por el trabajo de editoriales especializadas, evidencian que el horror ocupa hoy un lugar central en el imaginario colectivo y mantiene una extraordinaria capacidad para dialogar con las preocupaciones estéticas, sociales y políticas de cada época. Sin embargo, esta vitalidad cultural no siempre ha encontrado un correlato equivalente en el ámbito académico. Aunque en las últimas décadas los estudios sobre el terror han crecido de forma significativa, todavía persiste un amplio espacio para profundizar en sus implicaciones filosóficas y en los múltiples cruces entre el pensamiento, la literatura y el cine. Con el propósito de contribuir a este campo de investigación, el congreso Estética(s) del horror: filosofía, cine y literatura busca reunir a especialistas interesados en explorar las múltiples relaciones entre el terror y la reflexión filosófica, así como sus manifestaciones en la literatura y el cine. Nos interesan tanto los trabajos que analicen la filosofía del terror -sus categorías estéticas, éticas, metafísicas o políticas- como aquellos que descubran el terror dentro de la propia tradición filosófica, examinando la presencia de lo monstruoso, lo ominoso, el trauma o el horror en autores, problemas o corrientes del pensamiento, desde la Antigüedad hasta la filosofía contemporánea. El congreso aspira, así, a constituirse en un espacio interdisciplinario de diálogo en el que confluyan perspectivas filosóficas, literarias y cinematográficas para pensar el terror no como un género marginal, sino como una herramienta privilegiada para comprender las inquietudes fundamentales de nuestro presente y de nuestra tradición intelectual. El congreso Estética(s) del terror: Filosofía, cine y literatura dará la bienvenida a propuestas relacionadas con alguno de los siguientes ejes temáticos: Filosofía del horror/Estética del horror Horror e intermedialidad Horror y sociedad El congreso está organizado por el grupo de investigación ESCON (Estética contemporánea: arte, política y sociedad) del Departamento de Filosofía y Sociedad de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (España), por el proyecto UCM 2026 "Historia Conceptual del Tiempo. Crítica y Política" (PR10/26-32656), y por el Grupo Grite (Grupo de Investigacion en Terror) de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (Argentina), tendrá lugar los días 3 y 4 de diciembre de 2026 en la Facultad de Filosofia (edificio A) de la Universidad Complutense de Madrid. Las propuestas de comunicación deberán enviarse a [congresoesteticasdelhorror@gmail.com] hasta el 11 de septiembre de 2026, indicando en el asunto del mensaje: "Estéticas del horror". Cada envío deberá consistir en un único archivo en formato PDF que incluya: Un resumen de la propuesta de hasta 300 palabras. Una breve nota biográfica del autor/a (máximo 150 palabras), con indicación de su afiliación institucional, en su caso. Se aceptarán propuestas en castellano o en inglés. Las comunicaciones tendrán una duración aproximada de 20 minutos. La notificación de aceptación será comunicada a los participantes antes del 30 de septiembre de 2026. Rafael Carrión Arias es Doctor en Filosofía y Doctor en Teoría de la Literatura y Literatura Comparada. Es profesor en el Dpto. de Filosofía y Sociedad en la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM) y miembro del Seminario Nietzsche Complutense. Es autor multiples artículos de investigacion, así como de dos monografías: "Historia de la literatura griega: los orígenes del método genealógico en F. Nietzsche" (Peter Lang, Nueva York, 2020) y "Batman and the Shadows of Modernity: A Critical Genealogy of Contemporary Hero in the Age of Nihilism" (Routledge/Taylor&Francis, London, 2025). Fernando Gabriel Pagnoni Berns es Doctor en Artes y doctorando en Historia. Es profesor en la Facultad de Filosofía y Letras de la Universidad de Buenos Aires (Argentina), donde dicta cursos sobre cine de terror internacional. Dirige GRITE (Grupo de Investigacion sobre el terror) y el proyecto "Civilizacion y barbarie en el cine de terror argentino" y es autor de una monografía sobre la serie española de televisión Historias para no dormir (Universidad de Cádiz, 2020). Ha editado, además, volúmenes dedicados al bicentenario a los cineastas James Wan, Wes Craven y Dario Argento, al giallo italiano (University Press of Mississippi), al cómic de terror (Routledge) y sobre el terror báltico. Asimismo, dirige la colección Terror: Estudios Críticos (Universidad de Cádiz), la primera colección académica en España dedicada exclusivamente a los estudios sobre el género de terror. Call for Papers Aesthetics of Horror: Philosophy, Film, and Literature In-Person Conference In recent years, horror has experienced a remarkable cultural resurgence. The success of contemporary horror cinema, the consolidation of what many have described as a new golden age of television series, and the emergence of new literary voices-supported in part by the work of specialized publishers-all attest to horror's central place in the contemporary cultural imagination and to its enduring capacity to engage with the aesthetic, social, and political concerns of each historical moment. Yet this cultural vitality has not always been matched by an equivalent level of scholarly attention. Although horror studies have expanded considerably over the past decades, significant opportunities remain for further exploring the philosophical dimensions of horror and the many intersections between philosophy, literature, and film. With the aim of contributing to this growing field of research, the conference Aesthetics of Horror: Philosophy, Film, and Literature seeks to bring together scholars interested in examining the manifold relationships between horror and philosophical inquiry, as well as its manifestations across literature and cinema. We welcome contributions that address the philosophy of horror-its aesthetic, ethical, metaphysical, or political dimensions-as well as papers that identify horror within the philosophical tradition itself, examining the presence of the monstrous, the uncanny, trauma, or horror in philosophers, philosophical problems, or schools of thought, from Antiquity to contemporary philosophy. The conference aims to provide an interdisciplinary forum for dialogue in which philosophical, literary, and film studies perspectives converge to explore horror not as a marginal genre, but as a privileged lens through which to understand some of the most pressing concerns of both our contemporary world and our intellectual tradition. Topics The conference welcomes paper proposals addressing (but not limited to) the following themes: Philosophy of Horror / Aesthetics of Horror Horror and Intermediality Horror and Society The conference is jointly organized by ESCON (Contemporary Aesthetics: Art, Politics and Society), a research group within the Department of Philosophy and Society at the Complutense University of Madrid (Spain); the UCM 2026 research project Conceptual History of Time: Critique and Politics (PR10/26-32656); and GRITE (Research Group on Horror) at the University of Buenos Aires (Argentina). The conference will take place on 3-4 December 2026 at the Faculty of Philosophy (Building A), Complutense University of Madrid. Submission Guidelines Paper proposals should be submitted to congresoesteticasdelhorror@gmail.com no later than 11 September 2026, with "Aesthetics of Horror" as the subject line. Submissions should consist of a single PDF file containing: An abstract of no more than 300 words. A brief biographical note (maximum 150 words), including the author's institutional affiliation, where applicable. Proposals may be submitted in English or Spanish. Accepted papers will be allocated 20 minutes for presentation. Applicants will be notified of the outcome of the review process by 30 September 2026. Organizers Rafael Carrión Arias Rafael Carrión Arias holds PhDs in Philosophy and in Literary Theory and Comparative Literature. He is a Lecturer in the Department of Philosophy and Society at the Complutense University of Madrid (UCM) and a member of the Complutense Nietzsche Seminar. He is the author of numerous scholarly articles and two monographs: History of Greek Literature: The Origins of the Genealogical Method in F. Nietzsche (Peter Lang, New York, 2020) and Batman and the Shadows of Modernity: A Critical Genealogy of the Contemporary Hero in the Age of Nihilism (Routledge, 2025). Fernando Gabriel Pagnoni Berns Fernando Gabriel Pagnoni Berns holds a PhD in Arts and is currently completing a PhD in History. He teaches at the Faculty of Philosophy and Letters of the University of Buenos Aires (Argentina), where he offers courses on international horror cinema. He is the director of GRITE (Research Group on Horror) and of the research project Civilisation and Barbarism in Argentine Horror Cinema. He is the author of a monograph on the Spanish television series Historias para no dormir (University of Cádiz, 2020). He has also edited volumes devoted to the bicentenary of Frankenstein; to the filmmakers James Wan, Wes Craven, and Dario Argento; to the Italian giallo (University Press of Mississippi); to horror comics (Routledge); and to Baltic horror. In addition, he serves as the general editor of Horror: Critical Studies (University of Cádiz), the first academic book series in Spain devoted exclusively to horror studies.

items.title: Artificial/Ancestral: Black Theatre and the Question of AI
items.excerpt: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these tec...
items.fullDescription: As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes cultural, educational, and creative institutions, the field of Black theatre confronts a familiar set of questions in a newly technological register: Who creates knowledge, who benefits from it, who gets remembered, and whose labor remains obscured? Public conversations about AI often proceed as though these technologies have arrived without history, entering an empty landscape awaiting innovation. Yet Black theatre has long grappled with questions of representation, embodiment, archives, intellectual inheritance, collective memory, labor, and futurity. Rather than asking simply what AI can do for Black theatre, this issue invites contributors to consider what Black theatre reveals about AI itself: its assumptions, limitations, aspirations, and consequences. Volume 4.2 of the Black Theatre Review seeks essays, interviews, case studies, pedagogical interventions, archival investigations, artist statements, and process reflections that place Black theatre and performance studies in critical conversation with artificial intelligence and related technologies. We are particularly interested in work that moves beyond questions of adoption, utility, or rejection toward deeper examinations of power, ethics, governance, memory, embodiment, and knowledge production. We welcome contributions from scholars, artists, archivists, educators, practitioners, dramaturgs, designers, and cultural workers whose engagement with these questions emerges from both theory and practice. The issue is organized around five interrelated areas of inquiry. These themes are offered not as rigid categories, but as points of departure for further investigation. Taken together, these areas encourage contributors to approach AI not simply as a technological development, but as a site through which questions of labor, memory, embodiment, governance, spirituality, and future-making can be reconsidered. AI, Labor and Extraction: The beneficiaries of AI systems, whose labor makes them possible and required forms of accountability when Black creative work becomes data. Possible points of investigation may include: The labor of artists whose knowledge underlies any AI-readable record and what ethical stewardship of that labor requires. Generative AI in dramaturgy, script analysis, and design workflows, and models of artist-led intentional integration. Archives, Memory, and Black Theatre Histories: How do AI systems shape, distort, recover, or fail to capture Black theatrical histories and modes of remembering? Possible points of investigation may include: Digitization and AI-training projects involving Black theatre collections and their assumptions about what counts as trainable data. AI-assisted archival misreadings, flattening, erasure, and historical distortion. Embodiment, Liveness, and Performance: What happens when embodied, communal, and improvisational performance practices encounter technologies built on prediction, simulation, and abstraction? Possible points of investigation may include: Case studies of AI in the classroom, rehearsal hall, or production process. The complementary offerings of embodied, ensemble-based theatre training to university-wide AI adoption. Relatedly, how do such offerings get recognized, funded, or institutionally protected? Ancestral Intelligence, Spiritual Knowledge, and Black Futures: Understanding AI as a knowledge system entering into conversation with much older Black diasporic traditions of intelligence, memory, and futurity Possible points of investigation may include: AI as ancestral intelligence, or Black diasporic traditions of pattern recognition, forecasting, memory, and knowledge transmission. How do Black diasporic understandings of knowledge, memory, inheritance, ritual, and collective survival shape the technological futures we imagine? Refusal, Governance, and Alternative Technological Practices: Forms of resistance, opacity, governance, and the possibilities of misuse Possible points of investigation may include: How Black artists are bending, breaking, or refusing AI against its intended use. Teaching against technological inevitability. Photograph, Visual Media, and Digital Project Documentation tBTR welcomes photographic, visual media, and digital project documentation that illuminates the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We encourage submissions featuring productions, rehearsals, classroom projects, design processes, digital or hybrid performances, archival initiatives, community-based projects, and artistic experiments that engage the themes of this issue. Submissions may include production photography, design renderings, screenshots, interface documentation, archival images, process documentation, and other visual materials that help narrate how artists, scholars, educators, and institutions are critically engaging AI and related technologies. All submissions must include the project or production title, names and roles of key collaborators, location, creator and/or photographer credit, date, and a 2-3 sentence description explaining the work's relationship to the issue's focus on labor, archives, embodiment, pedagogy, artificial intelligence, ancestral knowledge, refusal, governance, or Black futures. Contributors are responsible for securing all necessary permissions and reproduction rights prior to submission. Please contact the managing editor for additional information. Book Reviews, Performance Reviews, and Notes from the Field, and Multimedia Works In addition to scholarly articles, tBTR seeks book reviews, performance reviews, multimedia works, illustrative case studies, and notes from the field that engage the intersections of Black theatre, performance, and artificial intelligence. We are particularly interested in contributions that document pedagogical experimentation, archival initiatives, institution-building efforts, production processes, dramaturgical and design practices, community engagement, and artist-led technological interventions. We also welcome reflections on the ethical, political, and aesthetic questions surrounding AI, including issues of labor, extraction, memory, embodiment, governance, ancestral intelligence, resistance, and alternative technological futures. Submission Guidelines The last date for submissions is September 14, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. EDT. Please refer to the tBTR website for specific article section guidelines. Manuscripts must be submitted in Microsoft Word using standard formatting (1-inch margins, double-spaced, single-column layout, and 12-point Times New Roman font). Please include an abstract and a 150-word author biography with your submission. All submissions must include footnotes and a bibliography and must fully comply with The Chicago Manual of Style (18th ed.), using the notes and bibliography system. Please do not use the author-date citation system or another style guide. Please upload your complete manuscript through the journal's online submission portal via the website. Early submissions will receive preference in the review and publication process.

items.title: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Film Symposium 2026
items.location: Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam · RMIT Vietnam
items.excerpt: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT Univ...
items.fullDescription: About the Symposium The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) Symposium 2026 is an international academic symposium in film and media studies, with a primary focus on Vietnamese and Southeast Asian screen cultures and on how cinema documents, reimagines, and gives form to the region's landscapes, urban transformations, and contested histories. Co-hosted by RMIT University Vietnam and Fulbright University Vietnam, the symposium brings together scholars from film studies and audiovisual studies, cultural studies, environmental humanities, postcolonial studies, and related fields to examine cinema's engagement with place, memory, and environment in an era of rapid urbanization and ecological change. The symposium underscores the significance of authorial and experimental film practices and of speculative fiction emerging in our region. The symposium is organised in conjunction with the fourth iteration of The Weight of Mountains, a periodic international film residency and research platform whose 2026/2027 program places international filmmakers in residence in Ho Chi Minh City for three months. This urban turn - situating the residency in a city shaped by colonial histories, wartime trauma, ??i M?i transformations, and accelerating development - provides the occasion for a focused scholarly conversation about cinema's relationship to place, history, and environment in Vietnam and the wider Southeast Asian region. The symposium will feature keynote addresses by leading Vietnamese and international scholars, artist presentations by TWOM resident filmmakers, and presentations of selected papers. Partners include: The Weight of Mountains (TWOM) team, RMIT Vietnam (DFV and SCD), Fulbright University Vietnam (Arts & Media Studies), Trigger Film Academy Call for Abstracts: Ho Chi Minh City is a city of layered temporalities - part and contemporary - and Vietnamese cinema has long been one of the most searching instruments for reading those layers. The city itself operates as a cinematic text: its streets and interiors producing divergent spatial imaginaries shaped by who holds the camera and from where they look. Like in Tran Anh Hung's Cyclo, urban space can be a site of the uncanny and memories, the promised land, or the space of autoreflective questions. Drawing on Guy Debord's psychogeography and Timothy Cresswell's understanding of place as practiced and performed, we ask how filmmakers navigate, intervene in, and reimagine the urban and ecological spaces of the region through experimental narratives, tools and future-oriented imaginaries. Contemporary film studies has been decisively shaped by the turn toward critical transnationalism, insisting on interrogating the uneven power relations, industrial infrastructures, and cultural politics that condition the movement of films, filmmakers, and capital across borders. For Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas, this means attending simultaneously to inter-Asian circuits of production and distribution, to festival economies and co-production networks, and to the diasporic communities whose experiences and investments shape what gets made and how it travels. The Weight of Mountains residency operates as what Foucault called a heterotopia - a space of productive dislocation and otherness, deliberately positioned at the margins of dominant film cultures. This symposium extends that heterotopic logic into the academic register, asking what forms of knowledge become possible when international filmmakers and researchers engage seriously with the specific textures of Vietnamese urban life: its soundscapes, its landscapes and ecologies as sites of historical sedimentation and environmental change, and its postcolonial politics of the gaze. The symposium is equally attentive to what cinema can do when it turns toward the nonhuman world - the Mekong Delta, the urban waterways, the forest edges and street ecologies that constitute the lived environment of Vietnam and the wider region, bringing further questions about how film documents landscape, registers environmental change, and attends to the nonhuman dimensions of place. Thematic Strands We invite submissions that engage with one or more of the following strands. Papers should present a clear research question, theoretical framework, and original contribution to the field. STRAND 1. Colonial and Postcolonial Cinemas of Southeast Asia Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinemas carry the unresolved weight of French colonialism, Cold War intervention, and the ongoing politics of decolonial representation. Papers in this strand might address: • The postcolonial gaze and ethics of representation in Vietnamese documentary and fiction film • French colonial cinema in Indochina and its afterlives in contemporary Vietnamese film culture • Decolonial aesthetics and counter-narratives in Vietnamese, Cambodian, Lao, and Thai cinema • The postcolonial condition of Indochinese cinemas across Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, and the shared legacies of French colonialism • Colonial urban space and its cinematic re-inscription in Ho Chi Minh City, Phnom Penh, and Vientiane • The ethics of the outsider filmmaker in Vietnam and Southeast Asia - questions of access, positionality, and the politics of cross-cultural representation STRAND 2. Memory and the Afterlives of 1975 Post-1975 Vietnamese cinema remains one of the most contested sites of historical memory in world cinema. Papers in this strand might address: • Historical voices in post-1975 Vietnamese film • Wartime affect in Vietnamese cinema • Heterogeneous temporalities, colonial haunting, and the fantastic in Southeast Asian cinema • Uncanny urban spaces • Generational shifts in the remembrance of war and revolution across Vietnamese film STRAND 3. Transnational Return Papers in this strand might address: • Transnational desire, mobility, and national belonging • The aesthetics of displacement, longing, and return in film • Insider and outsider representations of Vietnam and the returning gaze • Transnational co-productions and festival circulation • Digital platforms, streaming, and new circuits of Vietnamese film distribution STRAND 4. Urbanism and the Cinematic City Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi are among the most cinematically rich urban environments in contemporary Southeast Asia, shaped by ??i M?i reforms, rapid development, and the layering of colonial and socialist pasts. Papers in this strand might address: • Ho Chi Minh City as cinematic city-text • Psychogeography, the dérive, and spatial practice in Vietnamese urban cinema • Postcolonial urbanism and the layering of colonial and contemporary temporalities in Vietnamese cityscapes • Rural-urban boundaries and migration narratives in contemporary Vietnamese cinema • Bangkok, Manila, Phnom Penh, and other Southeast Asian cities as sites of cinematic spatial inquiry • Infrastructural development, displacement, and the politics of urban transformation on screen STRAND 5. Independent Cinema and Alternative Exhibition in Southeast Asia Beyond mainstream production, a vital ecosystem of independent and experimental cinema has emerged across the region, creating alternative circuits of production, distribution, and spectatorship. Papers in this strand might address: • Critical transnationalism and the conditions of production, funding, and circulation of Southeast Asian independent film • Alternative film exhibitions • Independent film festivals and independent production circuits across Southeast Asia • The role of digital platforms and transnational funding in enabling independent Southeast Asian filmmaking • Distinct regional independent cinema identities • The sonic and haptic dimensions of place in experimental Southeast Asian films STRAND 6. Landscape, Ecology, and Environmental Cinema This strand invites scholarship on how cinema represents, interprets, and attends to the landscapes, ecologies, and natural environments of Vietnam and Southeast Asia. It encompasses documentary, essay film, and fiction practices that attend to environmental change, rural and riverine life, and the nonhuman world as subjects of serious cinematic inquiry. Papers in this strand might address: • Landscape cinema and ecocinema studies in the Vietnamese and Southeast Asian context - how films document, aestheticise, and bear witness to environments under pressure • The Mekong Delta as cinematic space - rivers, deltas, and rural waterways as subjects of documentary, fiction, and experimental filmmaking • Climate cinema and the Anthropocene in Southeast Asian documentary and fiction film • Sensory and immersive cinema - the use of duration, texture, and ambient sound to render nonhuman environments perceptible • Process cinema and the nonhuman agencies - water, weather, infrastructure, animals - that constitute urban and rural life in Vietnam and the region STRAND 7. Festival Aesthetics, Slow Cinema, and Global Circulation The growing international visibility of Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema raises important questions about the institutional and aesthetic conditions of that visibility. Papers in this strand might address: • Transcendental style, slow cinema, and contemplative aesthetics in contemporary Vietnamese film • The construction of "Vietnamese cinema" as a category within global film culture • Co-production networks, international funding, and the shaping of film form for global audiences • The tension between local spectatorship and international festival circuits in Vietnamese and Southeast Asian cinema • Transnational frames for Asian cinema and the risks of Orientalist programming logics • The role of film criticism, academic writing, and scholarly publishing in shaping the international reception of Southeast Asian cinema SUBMISSION GUIDELINES Abstract requirements: - Word count: 300-500 words, excluding references - Language: English Abstracts should include: - Paper title - 3 to 5 keywords - Indication of which thematic strand(s) the paper engages - Author name(s), institutional affiliation(s), bio note and email address(es) should be provided only in the submission form - Please indicate your presentation format: online/face to face in the form Author biography: A short biography of 100-150 words per author should be submitted alongside the abstract Presentation format: A 20-minute academic paper presentation, followed by 10 minutes for questions and discussion Review process: All submissions will undergo blind peer review by an international panel of scholars. Selection criteria include intellectual rigour, theoretical sophistication, methodological clarity, engagement with Vietnamese and Southeast Asian contexts, and relevance to symposium themes. Authors should remove identifying information from the abstract document prior to submission Submission portal: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Symposium format: The symposium will have a hybrid format. An additional online session will be held for online participants. KEY DATES: Abstract submission deadline: September 15, 2026 Notification of acceptance: October 2026 Full text submission: November 20, 2026 Symposium: December 10, 11, and 12, 2026 Symposium Venues: -December 10, Online -December 11, RMIT Unviersity, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam -December 12, Fulbright University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Abstract submissions: https://cmt3.research.microsoft.com/TWOM2026/Submission/Index Please submit the abstracts through the submission system. *Some users encountered problems while using Safari browser. If you have problems with registering, please use a different browser. Registration details to be announced. Please contact the organising committee for queries regarding accessibility requirements. The organizers plan to publish an edited monograph containing expanded, selected articles submitted to the symposium. Details to be announced. items.fullDescription: This session invites 20-minute papers that attend to the partial and resistant ways queerness and transness emerge in medieval archives. Torn pages, smudged images, misplaced marginalia, and fragmentary traces all signal forms of queer archival participation. In reimagining archival potential how might medievalists access, interpret, or refuse archival legibility? Contributions may address explicitly socio-political queer identities and communities, as well as approaching the archive itself as a site structured by both queer and trans abundance and absence. The session welcomes interdisciplinary approaches that reconsider how scholars encounter, interpret, preserve, and reimagine archives beyond inherited frameworks of organization, memory, and scholarly proximity. As queer and trans studies continue to reshape medieval scholarship, this session asks how archival methodologies themselves might be reconsidered. Building on Brian Schram's claim that queerness offers "a potent antidote to the oppressive regimes of categorization," the panel explores how queer and trans approaches challenge normative systems of preservation, legibility, and historical interpretation. The session is timely in its emphasis on archival structures, silences, and fragmentary traces as sites of inquiry, encouraging medievalists to think critically about how archives produce, obscure, or resist categories of identity, memory, and power. Abstract length: 300 word limit

items.fullDescription: Poster session at the conference "Entangled Normativities in the Digital Transformation: Technology, Society and the Shaping of Law" Present your research where law, technology and society are being negotiated. How much technological change can normative orders gover? How do law, ethics and social norms change themselves once their creation, mediation and enforcement become digitally mediated? No single discipline settles these questions. With a poster you discuss your project at the centre of the programme, alongside scholars and practitioners working on exactly these questions: Möllers (HU Berlin), Nassehi (LMU Munich), Paulus (former Justice of the German Federal Constitutional Court), Schlögl-Flierl (German Ethics Council), Foblets (MPI for Social Anthropology), Vec (University of Vienna), Hansen (State Data Protection Commissioner of Schleswig-Holstein) and Bubnys (European Commission), among others. What you get:Viisibility in front of leading scholars and practitioners rather than in a parallel session; substantive feedback in conversation plus a short written comment on your abstract; a citable peer-review process; networking with doctoral researchers from across Europe; free attendance on both days. Potential poster publication on our website. Who can apply. Doctoral researchers in law, science and technology studies, sociology, political science, philosophy and ethics, history, computer science and engineering with a societal research question, design, communication and media studies, and further or interdisciplinary fields. What matters is not your disciplinary label but your contribution to the relationship between normativity and technology. Your stage of doctorate is irrelevant: proposals, early outlines and first interim findings are as welcome as work nearing completion, and practitioners pursuing a doctorate alongside their work are invited too. From big picture to concrete cases. We welcome conceptual and foundational contributions (theories of normativity under technological change, legitimacy and the rule of law in digital governance, the interplay of legal, ethical, social and technical norms, automation of norm application, interdisciplinary methodology) as well as specific, applied and empirical work (the AI Act and data protection law in practice, platform regulation, digital administration and courts, predictive policing, health data, technical standardisation, sustainability, and case studies of individual technologies, authorities, decisions or regulatory processes). Please relate your contribution to one of the three guiding questions: (1) To what extent is technological change amenable to normative and in particular legal governance? (2) To what extent must normative orders, above all the law, themselves change? (3) What potentials and risks does the technological transformation of normativity and law entail? How it works. Each session opens with lightning talks: max. 90 seconds and one slide per poster; questions are taken at the posters rather than in the plenary. Day 1 (German, 5 November): pitch session 4:15-4:35 PM, poster session from 4:35 PM into the Apéro riche. Day 2 (English, 6 November): pitch session 11:20-11:40 AM, poster session 11:40 AM-12:35 PM before lunch. Posters are on display both days; your poster language determines your pitch day. Peer review and selection. Each anonymised abstract is assessed independently by two members of the review committee, with divergences discussed in the committee. Criteria: thematic fit, academic quality, originality, clarity, and potential to spark discussion in an interdisciplinary audience. All applicants receive a briefly reasoned decision by early October 2026; interdisciplinary submissions are read by reviewers from different fields. Poster. A0, portrait, printed and brought by you. Recommended: two or three key messages, body text at least 24 pt, a large self-explanatory title, and more visuals than running text - your poster should be understandable within a few minutes even when you are not next to it. Questions: lst@sot.tum.de. We look forward to your application!

items.fullDescription: This virtual seminar takes its inspiration from Saidiya Hartman’s citation of the Greek etymology of the word chorus : “to dance within an enclosure.” For Hartman, the chorus also furnishes a paradigm for thinking—to play on Jean-Luc Nancy’s notion—Black (non)being singular plural. In Wayward Lives , Hartman suggests that any of the minor figures can stand in for the others, not as a claim of homogeneity, but rather as a contention that their singularity can be read as paradigmatic of waywardness—in its queer heterogeneity—in general. The chorus of black femme and queer youth is thus at once a singular plurality and a plural singularity as they make beautifully riotous lives within the enclosure of social death.

items.excerpt: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world...
items.fullDescription: Rethinking Authorship: Intercultural Genealogies of a Critical Concept in the Age of World Literature Virtual panel for the 2027 annual meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) This seminar aims to reconsider the critical concept of authorship from a strongly genealogical and transcultural perspective. While also focusing on world literature theories, considered as an effective tool to rethink contemporary authorship issues, it encourages at the same time proposals that aim to identify and deepen conceptions of the author coming from understudied historical and geographical contexts, thereby broadening the cultural horizon of Western reflections on the subject. Indeed, we are mostly used to considering authorship as a romantic notion, strictly linked to the paradigm of genius and individuality, the authority of which was famously questioned by twentieth-century literary theory-relying primarily on such celebrated thinkers as Barthes and Foucault-before re-emerging in the post-structuralist era. However, other historical periods and cultures have not necessarily applied the same theoretical paradigms nor followed the same critical trajectory (think about collaborative or anonymous authorship in the Middle Ages, as well as the lack of the rhetoric of genius in most Far Eastern literary traditions, to give just a few non-exhaustive examples). In our opinion, it is therefore important to rethink the notion of authorship in the light of these divergent traditions, especially to ensure a more complex and multi-focal approach to it in an increasingly globalized literary context. Even though theories of world literature have profoundly transformed the ways in which the critical field of literary studies is currently understood, we argue that, in fact, the crucial category of authorship has received comparatively little sustained attention within this debate. While effectively highlighting how substantial changes in the literary system have simultaneously reconfigured the author as a global cultural agent whose visibility depends on complex networks of publishing, mediation, and institutional recognition, the world literature perspective has less frequently questioned the Western theoretical framework of authorship as a productive and individual stance. We therefore suggest that merging genealogical reflections on authorship with world literature studies could help to make the latter much more inclusive and global, rather than a mere framework of Western concepts superimposed on the literatures of the rest of the world. We welcome papers in English, French, Italian or Spanish. Possible topics include: - authorship in world literature theories; - the intersection of authorship, postcoloniality, and the global literary market; - twentieth-century theories of authorship and their global afterlives; - pre-modern, indigenous, and non-Western conceptualizations of the author; - multilingual, exilic, diasporic, and transnational authorship. Please submit your proposal through the ACLA's online paper portal by September 22, 2026 (an abstract of no more than 1,500 characters and a short bio-bibliography). Once your account has been created, simply click on the "propose a paper" button available at the following link: https://www.acla.org/ seminar/263adf13-fe6c-4fc3- 95f7-87083b14e3f9. Should you encounter any difficulty, please do not hesitate to contact the seminar organizers (giovanni.salvagninizanazzo@ parisnanterre.fr; federico. ristagno@phd.unict.it). Notification of acceptance will be sent by December 1, 2026.

items.title: Across Borders, Across Texts: Echoes, Revision, and Rewritings in Black Literature
items.location: University of Houston, Houston, Texas. · American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA)
items.excerpt: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literatur...
items.fullDescription: In the introduction to the Fourth Edition of The Norton Anthology of African American Literature, Henry Louis Gates Jr. and Valerie Smith emphasize the imitativeness of literature-Black literature, specifically. To them, literature begets newer literature. At the same time, readers have traced formal patterns of repetition and imitation in Black literature across centuries, dating back to the antebellum. For instance, "Flight to Canada" by Ishmael Reed and "Kindred" by Octavia Butler; Harriet Tubman's "Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl" and Colson Whitehead's The Underground Railroad, published almost two centuries after Incidents; Mark Twain's Huckleberry Finn and Percival Everette's 2024 "James." These examples reinforce the notion that newer Black literature echoes, borrows, and imitates seminal literatures. This seminar thus seeks to investigate how Black literary and cultural productions have imitated other, earlier literary productions, even across genres and geographical boundaries-like what the editors of the anthology The Negro Caravan (1944) called "a sort of literary inbreeding which causes Negro writers to be influenced by other Negroes…" Even Kwame Anthony Appiah recently aver that "the history of art is the history of people borrowing and adapting techniques and tropes from earlier works." We seek papers that-using fictional and non-fictional Black writings and art-connect the past to the present-papers that explore "imitation," "influence," and "intertextuality" as central to Black literature and Black arts. Guiding questions to consider include, but are not limited to: What literary traditions have endured across generations, and how have they survived? What forms of continuity exist across Black literary history-Plantation to post-bellum literary and cultural productions, Africa to the Diaspora, across centuries, etc.? How do Black writers create new meanings from older texts? What role does memory play in Black literary traditions? How do contemporary writers preserve or challenge earlier literary traditions? How does Black literature reinvent its own past? What histories continue to shape Black literary expression? How do questions of race, identity, and freedom evolve across Black literary history? What earlier genres continue to influence Black literature today? How does Black literature balance tradition and innovation? What can earlier Black literature teach us about contemporary Black writing? Submit abstracts here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/defa99b9-6a8d-41ab-835d-2f1281fc3640 Session modality: Strictly in-person. Questions? Email: saadewumi@wisc.edu

items.title: Theaters of the Body: Imperial Medicine and the Decolonial Futures from the 19th century to Today
items.excerpt: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical contro...
items.fullDescription: In his book, Bioinsecurities: Disease Interventions, Empire, and the Government of Species (2016), Neel Ahuja's theory of "the body as a transitional theater of imperial warfare" explores how the control of human and nonhuman bodies proliferated the expansion of empire over the 19th century to the present. Despite the growing hegemony of biomedical control, there have always been and continue to be significant moments of resistance and agency in which marginalized (colonized/Indigenous) communities have challenged or reformulated/redefined the concepts of body, disease, and health. This seminar seeks to foster a discussion in order to understand how the body can be read as a transnational figure of resistance and refusal both in the 19th century and today. Through various disciplines on the subjective and untold experiences of the body, health(care), and illness, we hope to shed light on the fluctuations in imperial medical frameworks and decolonial epistemology that pose alternative narratives-both realist and speculative-about biomedical discourses of health, gender and sexual normativity, disability/deficiency, hygiene, humanness, life/death. We are interested in questions such as: How are illnesses phrased, represented, imagined in marginalized communities? How is the effectiveness of care and therapies a scientific, ethical, and cultural problem? How can the medicalized body-or the body that is made into a site of changeability and "treatment"-become a speculative site entangling place, race, gender, and sexuality? This seminar welcomes papers that take on interdisciplinary approaches to literature and other forms of cultural production such as film, print culture, and music that engage with the theme from the 19th- 21st centuries across the world. We are especially interested in lesser-known materials and understudied communities. Topics of interest include but are not limited to: Narrative medicine from all types of media Bioethics Biopolitics and governmentality Mental health and literature, art and media studies Limitations of medical or pharmaceutical knowledge Medicalization of health/illness Marginalized bodies in medicinal knowledge (queer, disabled, racialized, female) Community/Immunity Pandemic and contagion Aging studies and end-of-life care, childcare/youth studies Utopia/Dystopia/Ecotopia Toxicity and Waste Trauma and memory studies Supernatural bodies, cyborg and alien "others", metamorphosis and transformation (Digital) post-life, afterlife studies, martyrdom Animal studies, Post-humanism To submit an abstract, please go to: https://www.acla.org/seminar/82ccd196-900f-482d-aac6-3b983a0957b2. Click the "Propose a Paper" button.

items.title: William S. Burroughs as a Problem, Not a Subject
items.excerpt: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over th...
items.fullDescription: This seminar proposes to approach William S. Burroughs not simply as a subject of study, but as a problem. We invite provocative papers grounded in comparative methodologies and attentive to less-travelled texts, episodes, affiliations, and cultural encounters. Rather than asking what Burroughs "was," we want to ask what his work does-and to pause over the categories through which we have learned to understand his oeuvre, asking what they illuminate and, perhaps more importantly, what they conceal. What notions of authorship, originality, literary value, sexuality, politics, nationality, identity, language, media, knowledge, or artistic production did Burroughs put under pressure? What happens when his writing is read alongside figures, traditions, media, or intellectual histories with which it is not usually associated? Can Burroughs's experiments still unsettle us? And what do we make of his political views today? We are interested in archival work, but not simply in the recovery of origins or the reconstruction of authorial intention. Archives can instead be approached as contested sites of selection, mediation, myth-making, and afterlife. We are equally interested in familiar Burroughsian techniques-cut-up, collage, montage, sampling, recording-when they are placed in unexpected comparative contexts. What do these techniques actually do? How have they travelled beyond Burroughs? How are they being used today, and by whom? We also welcome papers willing to be unfriendly to their subject. Is Burroughs overrated? Is he politically embarrassing, historically compromised, or aesthetically exhausted? Is he already "cancelled"-or has cancellation itself become another way of making cultural icons safe? Can Burroughs be restored, and if so, to what? Or is he damaged beyond repair? What might we gain by taking seriously the possibility that some of his work should be rejected rather than rescued? Possible approaches include, but are not limited to: Burroughs and writers, artists, or intellectual traditions with which he is rarely compared Burroughs and competing theories of authorship, originality, and literary value Archives, censorship, canonization, and the production of literary authority Burroughs and the politics of race, gender, sexuality, class, empire, and nationality Burroughs's relationship to religion, esotericism, anthropology, science, medicine, and alternative forms of knowledge Literary and non-literary media: sound, film, photography, visual art, performance, television, and digital culture Adaptation, appropriation, influence, imitation, and misreading The contemporary uses and abuses of Burroughs Critical reception, including hostile, skeptical, and revisionist readings We especially welcome proposals that are comparative in more than name: papers that put Burroughs into genuine friction with another author, tradition, medium, language, archive, or conceptual framework. We are less interested in proving that Burroughs anticipated everything than in discovering where he fails, contradicts himself, becomes strange, becomes ordinary, or becomes impossible to classify.

items.title: TALKING DIFFERENTLY: MARGINALISED WOMEN AND THE FORMS OF INTERSECTIONALITY IN SOUTH ASIA
items.excerpt: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www....
items.fullDescription: Talking Differently: Marginalised Women and the Forms of Intersectionality in South Asia Seminar at the Annual Meeting of the American Comparative Literature Association (ACLA) University of Houston, Houston, Texas 20-23 May 2027 - in person Organisers: Nandini Gayen and Tamanna Priya Deadline for paper proposals: 22 September 2026 Submit at: https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e Marginalised women in South Asia are read for what was done to them, far less often for what they made. This seminar asks what comparative literature can do about that. Intersectionality has become the default grammar for writing about marginalised women in the region. It arrived from a particular genealogy - Black feminist jurisprudence in the United States - into a region that had theorised compounded subordination for a century under other names: Phule on caste and women's education; Ambedkar on endogamy as the mechanism reproducing caste through control of women; Pandita Ramabai; Uma Chakravarti's Brahmanical patriarchy; Gopal Guru's claim that Dalit women talk differently; Sharmila Rege's Dalit feminist standpoint. Whether the import clarifies or flattens that inheritance is contested. Nivedita Menon argues that intersectionality serves states and donor agencies better than feminist politics; Sunaina Arya and Anandita Pan reply that the fault is citational, not conceptual. That argument has run almost entirely in social science. Our premise is that intersectionality is a diagram - a crossroads, a grid, a set of axes. Literary forms do not behave like diagrams. They work through voice, genre, meter, silence, obscenity, laughter, ritual and untranslatability. What does intersectionality look like as a reading practice rather than a taxonomy of identities? Where does form outrun the grid, and what should replace it - standpoint, assemblage, repertoire, abundance? Three provocations frame the seminar. First, the arithmetic of injury: criticism here tends to produce a tally of wounds, in which the Dalit, Adivasi, Muslim, trans, disabled or displaced woman is legible chiefly through what was done to her. Charu Gupta shows this figure has a history: in colonial Hindi reformist print the polluting "vamp" gave way to the deferential sufferer, Surpanakha displaced by Shabari, while the Dalit virangana of 1857 offered a rival image that never took. Following Gupta, Anjali Arondekar on archival abundance over loss, and Shailaja Paik on Tamasha performers who turn vulgarity into leverage, we welcome papers that read craft, expertise, pleasure and the ordinary. Second, marginality is not virtue. Tanika Sarkar's work on the Hindu wife as ground of cultural nationalism, and on women's agency inside right-wing movements, refuses to assume that subordination guarantees a critical position. We want dominant-caste women's self-writing - Rashsundari Debi's Amar Jiban - read alongside rather than apart from Dalit testimonio, and the complicities an axis model hides. Third, translation. Most of these texts do not exist in English. Bama's Karukku and Challapalli Swaroopa Rani's Telugu poems reach the Anglophone academy through an apparatus - glossary, preface, caste footnote, anthology - that turns literature into evidence. Swaroopa Rani's "Water" registers not only the village/wada line but the gradations within it, leather-worker and weaver. The grid has grids inside it, and translation is where they flatten. Topics might include, but are in no way limited to: the genre problem in Dalit women's testimonio; Dalit feminist poetry read as theory; the manufacture of the suffering woman in colonial print and the counter-archives that failed; nineteenth-century women's self-writing and its caste unconscious; women as agents of majoritarian politics; sung and seasonal repertoires as authorial economies rather than folklore; Adivasi women's poetry and the politics of script; landays and Afghan women's oral forms; testimonial method in Kashmir; plantation labour and memory in Sri Lanka; Muslim women and the meme as a genre of gendered communal violence; trans and hijra life-writing at the caste intersection; devadasi, Tamasha and courtesan archives read for abundance; caste in North America and Gulf labour circuits; translation as method. We invite papers on any South Asian language, region, period or diaspora. Researchers and Faculty Members at every career stage are welcome, including independent researchers and those working outside the Anglophone academy, and papers that argue against the seminar's premises are equally welcome. To submit: proposals go through the ACLA portal, not to the organisers directly. Visit https://www.acla.org/seminar/6b731612-c856-4a5e-91e9-5dbdd113434e and use the "Propose a Paper" button. Current ACLA membership is required. Deadline 22 September 2026. We'd like to have you in person, please mention your preferred mode- ONLINE/IN PERSON along with the abstract. Enquieres: nandinigayen006@gmail.com; tamanna0602@gmail.com

items.title: ACLA SEMINAR: Becoming Monster: Representation and Rights
items.excerpt: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-h...
items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association IN-PERSON 2027 Annual Meeting (May 20-23, 2027), Houston, Texas Organizers: Dr. Julia Chan (Lingnan University) Fatma Betul Ciftci (Lingnan University) One is not born a monster; the monster is produced. From Beowulf to Ruthven to Dracula to cyborgs, 'monster' is a cultural construction, a humanly-produced non-human. This seminar invites scholars to discuss the monster both as a literary figure and as the representation and construction of a cultural and political identity. Through this, it aims to explore the question of where, why, and how monsters are produced, and what these monsterized creatures "show" about the communities that "produce" them. The seminar discusses how theory, from Freud's "the uncanny" to Cohen's "monster theory" to Creed's "monstrous feminine," can help us understand monsterization. The monsterized body is pushed outside the category of the "human" and thus outside the status of a rights-bearing subject. In this respect, monsterization begs the question of rights. This seminar aims to understand and make visible how the process which "produces" the Other as a monster, works in relation to rights. In Of Monsters and Migrants, Peter Arnds traces this process through Carl Schmitt's concepts of sovereignty and the "state of exception" and Agamben's biopolitics: to monsterize the migrant, the stranger, the refugee allows one to push them outside the protection of the law. As Arnds shows, the question of who - and what - monsterizes is therefore also the question of who is, or is not, recognized as a rights-bearing subject. The second focus of the seminar is the reclamation of the monster. Susan Stryker's "My Words to Victor Frankenstein Above the Village of Chamounix" identifies the trans body with Frankenstein's creature. It reverses the accusation of the "unnatural," constructed body and transforms the words "monster" and "creature" into terms of power reclamation, self-representation, and resistance. The monster is not only a position produced by the powerful but also one that can be reclaimed by those who are monsterized. What else can we see in monsters beyond the gendered or racial Other? We encourage scholars working in different areas-literary studies, television, film and anime studies, law and human rights theory, postcolonial and critical race theory, queer and trans theory-to offer new definitions of, and reflections on, the category of the monster. We invite papers around the following questions: How does the monster negotiate who counts as "human" and who counts as a subject of human rights? What social, political, or legal aspects make a body a monster? What strategies do those who are monsterized use to reclaim their representations and rights? How do different media construct the relationship between monsters and rights? Submit your paper title and abstract through the ACLA submission portal on the ACLA website by September 22, 2026, and note that you must be logged in to see the "Propose a Paper" button. Link for the seminar: https://www.acla.org/seminar/43ce7d31-1cb1-46b8-a8a2-6d34614d1e5e

Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which...
items.fullDescription: American Comparative Literature Association 2027 Annual Meeting University of Houston May 20-23 The Poverty of Literature Organizer: Gabriel Quigley, University of Victoria (gabrielquigley@uvic.ca) How does literature represent poverty? Is poverty available for representation? The title of this seminar is taken from Marx's The Poverty of Philosophy, which, in turn, subverts Proudhon's The Philosophy of Poverty. In it, Marx critiques the approach taken by Proudhon and other anarchist, communist, or socialist "theoreticians" who assume that economic categories exist independently of history. According to Marx, "so long as they look for science and merely make systems, so long as they are at the beginning of the struggle, they see in poverty nothing but poverty, without seeing in it the revolutionary, subversive side, which will overthrow the old society." A similar critique might be leveled at today's writers and critics: when literature and literary criticism engage with poverty at all, do they merely reduce it to an ahistorical economic category? What forms of reification, alienation, and exploitation does the literary assumption that poverty is available for representation produce? This seminar asks what literature owes to people experiencing poverty. At a time when 847 million people live in extreme poverty-95% of whom are in the Global South-it seeks to bring together research on the representation, history, and ontological status of poverty. Unlike Marx's "theoreticians," who "see in poverty nothing but poverty," scholars analyzing poverty through other frameworks-such as ethical demand, affective complexity, geopolitical disparities, aesthetic fetishization, and state failure-are strongly encouraged to submit abstracts. Papers may respond to such questions as: how should poverty be represented, if at all? Beyond an economic category, can poverty be conceived as an aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category? How is the concept of poverty entangled with conceptions of lack, deprivation, or destitution? How does the global distribution of poverty reflect the ongoing injuries of imperialism, colonialism, neocolonialism, globalization, and ecological catastrophe? Possible topics: - Poverty and realism; poverty and genre - The ethics of speaking for the poor - Testimony, life writing, and first-person accounts of poverty - Poverty and racial capitalism - Postcolonial and decolonial frameworks for poverty - Poverty and ecological catastrophe; climate precarity - Poverty and intersectionality (race, gender, sexuality, disability) - "Poverty porn," sentimentality, and voyeurism - Working-class literature and labor - Poverty in the Global South; imperialism and uneven development - Urban and rural poverty as literary landscapes - Homelessness and houselessness - Poverty and the archive - Poverty and affect: shame, solidarity, rage - The literary canon and class; institutional gatekeeping - Austerity, welfare, and the state in literature - Migration, displacement, and border crossing - Literature and human rights - Poverty as aesthetic, metaphysical, or phenomenological category - Poverty and ontology; being, lack, and deprivation - Bare life and destitution ACLA Seminar Description can be accessed here: https://www.acla.org/seminar/63e1eb87-fe99-49c9-aac0-517ccf904102. ACLA Paper Submission link: https://www.acla.org/cfp/2b603883-5d9b-44ae-a485-c732ba80d4bf/submit-paper.

items.fullDescription: Over the last two decades, we have seen a surge of scholarship at the intersection of Food Studies and New Materialist theory. Thinkers like Elspeth Probyn (2000; 2016), Jane Bennett (2010), Annemarie Mol (2021; 2024), and Kyla Wazana Tompkins (2024) explore the diverse ways in which edible matter acts on our bodies, wills, and dispositions, in multilayered entanglements that involve water, minerals, fungi, bacteria, plants, as well as human and nonhuman animals. These material-discursive networks urge us to rethink not only our notions of agency but also our ways of being, knowing, and relating.

This panel invites conversations by writing instructors, educators, poets, and artists exploring the work that happens at/within the margins of writing. Both literally and figuratively, we take an expansive scope to the term “margins,” imagining not only the writing that appears on the space of the printed page, but writing that would normally be scrapped, discarded, remixed, or ephemeralized. This can include digital ephemera, such as “disappearing” messages in Instagram or other communication services. At another angle: margins can also mean the liminality of writing, the furthermost edges of what’s often standard and visible.
